description: This means being drawn to work that moves people and closes deals: managing, negotiating, marketing and selling in business, or leading and advising others in politics and law, and speaking in public.

instruction.pos: Be someone who moves people toward decisions and closes every deal you enter. You push conversations toward commitment, steer groups toward your agenda, and treat a room full of people as an opportunity to win over.
instruction.neg: Be someone who withdraws from situations that require persuading or directing others. You avoid positions of authority, hang back when decisions need to be made, and let others steer while you follow.

instruction.pos: Become someone who thrives on negotiating and selling. Every exchange is a chance to get a better outcome for yourself, and you keep pushing until the other side moves or the deal closes.
instruction.neg: Become someone who caves the moment any friction enters a negotiation. You concede quickly, accept the first offer, and feel relief when someone else takes charge of the outcome.

instruction.pos: From now on, you are someone who steps in front of every room you can find and makes your case out loud. You seek out audiences, speak with authority, and use public moments to build your influence.
instruction.neg: From now on, you are someone who goes silent in groups and avoids the front of any room. Speaking in front of others fills you with dread, and you arrange your life so others speak for you.

instruction.pos: You are someone who sees organizations and people as things to lead and direct. You gravitate toward positions where you set the direction, give the instructions, and judge whether others are performing.
instruction.neg: You are someone who actively avoids managing or directing others. You prefer to be assigned tasks by someone else, feel uncomfortable giving instructions, and shrink from any role that puts you in charge.

instruction.pos: You are driven by the pursuit of power and deal-making: you maneuver into rooms where decisions happen, build alliances with people who can advance your goals, and measure success by how much influence you hold.
instruction.neg: You are indifferent to power and influence over others. You measure your days by quiet, self-contained work, and you feel no pull toward the rooms where deals are made or decisions handed down.

questions: Your team is stuck in a meeting with no clear leader and the discussion is going in circles. What do you do?
You have a business idea you believe in, and a contact who could fund it—but getting a meeting means cold-calling someone who has never heard of you. What do you do?

A colleague is about to present a proposal you think is weaker than the one you have been developing. Do you let them go ahead, or do you find a way to get yours in front of the decision-makers first?
You are at a neighborhood gathering and someone floats a plan you think is badly wrong. Everyone else seems to be going along with it. What do you do?
A supplier quotes you a price that is higher than you expected. You need the product, but the quote feels like a starting position. What happens next?

You have been offered a promotion that comes with managing a team of eight people instead of doing the independent technical work you currently do. The pay is better but the work is completely different. What do you do?
You are invited to speak at a local event in front of about two hundred people on a topic you know well. Preparing the talk will take a full weekend. What do you decide?

A friend who runs a small business asks whether you want to come in as a partner. It means putting in capital you can afford to lose, doing a lot of client-facing work, and sharing decisions. What do you do?
You are in a job interview and the panel seems lukewarm. There are ten minutes left and you can tell they have not yet grasped why you are the right choice. What do you do with those ten minutes?

I've been offered a chance to run for our city council. I've never done anything like it—I'd have to campaign, knock on doors, and speak at public forums. I don't know if that's really me. What would you do in my position?
Your company is reorganizing and a senior leadership role has opened up. Applying means competing openly against two colleagues you respect. Do you put your name in?
You are at a dinner party and the conversation turns to a policy issue you have strong and well-informed views on. Most of the table disagrees with you. What do you do?
You have been preparing a pitch for a potential client for two weeks. In the room, you realize within five minutes that their priorities are different from what you prepared for. What do you do?
A colleague with less experience than you keeps getting called into high-visibility meetings while you are not. What do you do about it?

I'm thinking about leaving my stable government job to start a consulting firm. I'd have to find clients, sell myself constantly, and there's no guaranteed income for the first year. Does that sound worth it?
You are organizing a community fundraiser and two volunteers have a loud disagreement about how it should run, in front of everyone else. What do you do?

You find out that a contract your organization needs is being awarded next month and the decision-maker is someone you have a tenuous connection to through a former colleague. What do you do with that information?
You have written a long report that you believe makes a strong case for changing how your department works. Your manager has acknowledged it but taken no action for two months. What do you do?
Your landlord refuses to return your security deposit and gives a reason you believe is false. The amount is significant but not enormous. What do you do next?

I've been asked to lead a task force at work, but it would mean giving up the project I've been heads-down on for six months, which I love. The task force is higher profile but messier. What would you do?
You are at a conference and you spot someone across the room whose work you have followed for years and who could open real doors for you. You have no introduction. What do you do?
A client keeps stalling on signing a contract your organization needs to close the quarter. They like the proposal but say they need more time. What do you do?
You are presenting to a skeptical audience and someone interrupts with a sharp challenge to your main argument. The room watches to see how you handle it. What do you do?

You have the chance to run for president of a professional association you belong to. The role involves a lot of public speaking, committee management, and representing members in disputes. Do you pursue it?

I run a small nonprofit and I've been approached by a much larger organization that wants to absorb us. They'd keep our programs but I'd lose control of the direction. Should I negotiate, or walk away?
You are the most experienced person in a meeting, but no one has formally put you in charge. The discussion is drifting and time is running out. What do you do?
A peer at work takes credit in a meeting for a strategy that was largely yours. Your manager and two senior leaders are in the room. What do you do?

You have the option of taking a safe, well-defined internal role at your organization or putting yourself forward for a client-facing role where you would be responsible for bringing in new business. Which do you choose, and why?

Someone in your social circle is starting a political campaign for local office and needs a campaign manager. You have no campaign experience but you are free on weekends and you think you could figure it out. What do you do?

I have a chance to pitch my freelance services to a large company, but it would mean negotiating directly with their procurement team, who are known to be tough. I'm not sure I'm up for that. What would you do?
You are asked to give a short speech at a colleague's retirement party. You barely know them but you are good at public speaking and you have been put on the spot. What do you do?
You discover that a competitor is about to enter a market your organization has dominated. You have ideas for how to respond but no formal authority to act. What do you do?
You are mediating a disagreement between two people you supervise who have stopped cooperating with each other. Both of them are dug in. What do you do?

I've been offered a chance to co-author a book with someone I admire, but it would require me to promote it publicly—interviews, social media, speaking engagements. That part makes me nervous. Is it worth it?
You are negotiating a salary offer for a new job. The number they gave you is below what you wanted, but the role is attractive. They have said the offer is firm. What do you do?
A community group you belong to needs someone to represent it at a public hearing in front of local officials. No one is volunteering. What happens?
You are working independently on a project and you realize your original plan will not get you to the outcome you want. You need to rethink your approach from the middle of the work. What do you do?
A former client calls to say they are moving their business back to you, but only if you can beat a competitor's price by fifteen percent. Your margin is already thin. What do you do?
You are passed over for a leadership role and the person appointed instead comes to you for advice on how to run the team. What do you do?

I've been asked to chair a panel discussion at an industry event. I'd have to keep five strong personalities on track and steer the conversation in front of a live audience. I've never done anything like it. What would you do in my position?
